walkthroughs.body_html:
Sustaining Ecosystems — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Sustaining Ecosystems brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Sustaining Ecosystems.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between random, stratified and systematic sampling?
options: All three sampling methods produce the same results.

Random: every member has equal chance of selection. Systematic: pick every nth item. Stratified: divide the population into groups and sample proportionally from each — ensures subgroup representation.
Weather refers to rain and climate refers to temperature.
Stratified sampling means picking samples from different strata of rock.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between weather and climate?
options: Weather refers to rain and climate refers to temperature.
Weather is short-term atmospheric conditions at a specific time and place; climate is the long-term (typically 30-year) average of weather patterns in a region.
Stratified sampling means picking samples from different strata of rock.
Weather happens outside and climate happens globally.

mcqs.q: How do hotspot volcanoes differ from subduction-zone volcanoes?
options: Hotspot volcanoes form at plate boundaries like all other volcanoes.
Stratified sampling means picking samples from different strata of rock.
Hotspot volcanoes are just very hot subduction volcanoes.
Hotspots are stationary mantle plumes that punch through plates anywhere (e.g. Hawaii), while subduction-zone volcanoes form along plate boundaries from melting subducted crust.
